original_value: This study proposes a home care system (HCS) based on a brain-computer interface (BCI) with a smartphone. The HCS provides daily help to motor-disabled people when a caregiver is not present. The aim of the study is two-fold: (1) to develop a BCI-based home care system to help end-users control their household appliances, and (2) to assess whether the architecture of the HCS is easy for motor-disabled people to use. A motion-strip is used to evoke event-related potentials (ERPs) in the brain of the user, and the system immediately processes these potentials to decode the user’s intentions. The system, then, translates these intentions into application commands and sends them via Bluetooth to the user’s smartphone to make an emergency call or to execute the corresponding app to emit an infrared (IR) signal to control a household appliance. Fifteen healthy and seven motor-disabled subjects (including the one with ALS) participated in the experiment. The average online accuracy was 81.8% and 78.1%, respectively. Using component N2P3 to discriminate targets from nontargets can increase the efficiency of the system. Results showed that the system allows end-users to use smartphone apps as long as they are using their brain waves. More important, only one electrode O1 is required to measure EEG signals, giving the system good practical usability. The HCS can, thus, improve the autonomy and self-reliance of its end-users.

result.paraphrase: The study presents a smartphone-based brain-computer interface home care system (HCS) that offers daily assistance to motor-disabled people when a caregiver is unavailable. Its goals are to build a BCI-driven HCS that enables end-users to control household appliances and to evaluate whether the system architecture is easy for motor-disabled users to operate. A motion-strip elicits event-related potentials (ERPs) in the user’s brain, which the system processes immediately to decode intent. It then converts these intentions into application commands and transmits them via Bluetooth to the user’s smartphone to place an emergency call or launch the relevant app to generate an infrared (IR) signal for controlling a household appliance. Fifteen healthy participants and seven motor-disabled participants, including one person with ALS, took part in the experiment. The mean online accuracy was 81.8% and 78.1%, respectively. Using the N2P3 component to distinguish targets from nontargets can improve system efficiency. The results indicate that users can operate smartphone apps with their brain waves, and that only a single O1 electrode is needed to record EEG signals, making the system highly practical. Consequently, the HCS can enhance end-users’ autonomy and self-reliance.
